summary: Defines three MIME content types for carrying EDI (electronic data interchange) business documents in email, since there are many EDI specifications. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules for attaching electronic business forms to email so the receiver knows what they are.

subtitle: Three MIME content types that let businesses send EDI interchanges as ordinary Internet email.

tldr.problem: Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) carries structured business transactions between trading partners, and email is a natural delivery path, but there was no standard way to wrap EDI data in MIME messages.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three MIME content types, Application/EDIFACT, Application/EDI-X12 and Application/EDI-consent, that wrap an unchanged EDI interchange as the body of a MIME message.
tldr.outcome: EDI can travel through Internet email and other MIME services. The RFC adds no security of its own, so sensitive interchanges need separate security services.

today: RFC 1767 is a Proposed Standard from March 1995, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on MIME as defined in RFC 1521.

sections.title: EDI Meets MIME
sections.content:
Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) is a way of conducting structured transactions between trading partners. On paper the delivery mechanism was the postal system, so electronic mail is a natural fit for electronic transactions. RFC 1767 lets formatted business interchanges be encapsulated within MIME messages. The basic building block it works with is the interchange.

The scope is narrow. The RFC covers only the encapsulation of EDI objects in the MIME environment. It changes nothing in those objects, whose syntax and semantics stay as defined by their primary specifications. It simply adds Internet email to the many carriage and exchange mechanisms EDI already uses.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo only puts business forms into an email envelope. It does not change the forms at all.

sections.title: Three Content Types
sections.content:
Since there are many different EDI specifications, the RFC sorts them into three categories, each with its own MIME content type.

  • Application/EDI-X12 for contents that conform to the specifications developed through the X12 standards organization.
  • Application/EDIFACT for contents that conform to the specifications of the United Nations Working Party 4 Group of Experts 1 EDIFACT boards.
  • Application/EDI-consent for all other specifications.

Each is registered in the same template form. The type name is Application, there are no required parameters, and the only optional parameter is CHARSET, as defined for MIME.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three stickers for the envelope: one for the X12 kind of form, one for the EDIFACT kind, and one for everything else.

sections.title: EDIFACT and X12 Body Parts
sections.content:
The Application/EDIFACT body part holds data exactly as specified for EDI by the EDIFACT documents. Application/EDI-X12 does the same for ASC X12 data. Both are described as a generic mechanism for sending any interchange of that family. The object is self-defining, meaning it indicates which specific EDI objects it contains, so the MIME type does not need to say.

Most EDI data is text, but some delimiters can be non-printable ASCII, and some data can be pure binary. For such objects the MIME transfer mechanism may need to use Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable or base64. The rationale given for both types is that these specifications are accepted standards for a class of inter-organization transactions, and this permits their transmission over the Internet by email.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope holds the form untouched, and the form says what it is. If the form has odd symbols that email might mangle, it is first rewritten in a safe code.

sections.title: The EDI-consent Type
sections.content:
Application/EDI-consent carries EDI data that two trading partners have explicitly agreed to exchange under a bilateral agreement. It only provides a standard way of wrapping the objects. It does not specify anything about what is inside.

The RFC says this traffic is substantial and well established, even though it falls outside the usual accredited standards world, and the type gives a standard way to delimit it. There is one firm rule: X12 and EDIFACT objects must be sent using their assigned MIME content types. EDI-consent is for all other EDI objects, and only according to trading partner agreements between the originator and the recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the catch-all sticker. It only works if the sender and receiver have already agreed in advance what the forms look like.

sections.title: A Sample Message
sections.content:
The RFC gives a short example of sending a single EDIFACT interchange. It stresses that real use needs attention to considerable detail and that the example only shows the gist. The message has the usual mail headers, a Mime-Version: 1.0 header, a Content-Type: Application/EDIFACT header and, here, Content-Transfer-Encoding: QUOTED-PRINTABLE, followed by the standard EDIFACT interchange as the body.

An appendix helps EDI users unfamiliar with email. It describes the user agent and mail transfer agent model and notes that the transmission steps replaced by Internet modules are the middle ones: MIME encapsulation, RFC 822 packaging, mail submission, SMTP relaying, delivery and stripping. The business program and EDI translator at both ends stay as they were.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a normal email with a different sticker on the envelope. The business form is in the letter part.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
EDI transactions typically include sensitive data, so transmission often needs to attend to authentication, data integrity, privacy, access control and non-repudiation. This specification makes it possible to send such data over Internet mail and other MIME-capable services, and it says that appropriate security services are essential for sensitive data.

The specification does not itself provide any security mechanism. Where needed, such mechanisms MUST be added, either through Internet MIME-based security services or any other suitable service, such as those provided by EDI-based standards.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope is not locked. If the form is private, you must add your own lock.

data.title: Single EDIFACT interchange
data.code:
To:  <<recipient organization EDI email address>>
Subject:
From: <<sending organization EDI email address>>
Date:
Mime-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: Application/EDIFACT
Content-Transfer-Encoding:  QUOTED-PRINTABLE

<<standard EDIFACT Interchange goes here>>
